title: Knowledge of past and future (3.16)
hook: the first of the powers in book three follows straight from yesterday: see how a thing changes, all the way, and you see where it came from and where it's going

segments.voice: Yesterday: the transformations of mind, and your line, what changes. Lump, pot, shards, and the clay all the way through. What did you catch changing? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

A forester cuts a slice from a fallen oak and counts the rings. This thin one, a dry year. This dark scar, a fire. These wide ones, good rain. She can read a hundred years of weather in a circle of wood. And if you ask her, she can tell you something about the years ahead too: how this stand of trees will grow, which ones will need light. She isn't psychic. She just understands, deeply, how wood changes. Book three is named Vibhuti, the book of powers. Today the powers begin, and the first one sounds like her.
screen: `A SLICE OF OAK.` → `A DRY YEAR, A FIRE, GOOD RAIN.` → `THE POWERS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.16: by samyama on the three transformations, knowledge of the past and the future. Remember the three from yesterday: change of property, change of time, change of condition. The lump becoming the pot. The future pot hidden in the clay, the past lump still in the pot. Patanjali's claim follows from that. If concentration, meditation and absorption rest fully on how a thing changes, the whole arc opens up: where it's been, where it's heading. The word for past is atita, what has gone by. Future is anagata, what has not yet come. You heard anagata a couple of weeks ago, in the pain not yet come, to be avoided. The word for these powers in general is siddhi, an accomplishment, a perfection, and this is the first of a long list. Over the next days Patanjali will name many: knowing other minds, strength, the inner map of the body, and stranger things. How are they meant? Within the tradition, many have taken them as real capacities that come with deep practice, and stories of sages are full of them. Others read them more inwardly, as pictures of what clear seeing makes possible. The sutras themselves list them plainly, without bragging, and before the list is done they'll add a warning, which we'll hear in its place. For now, notice how ordinary the first power's logic is. It isn't magic fire. It's the forester's eye, taken all the way. Understanding change so completely that time opens in both directions.
screen: `SAMYAMA ON THE THREE CHANGES.` · `ATITA AND ANAGATA: PAST AND FUTURE.` · `SIDDHI: AN ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `REAL POWER, OR CLEAR SEEING?` · then, large: `THE POWERS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice reads one small arc. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Then bring to mind one object near you, a mug, a plant, your own hand. Ask quietly: where did this come from? Clay, a seed, your parents. Where is it going? Shards, compost, age. No need for answers you can't know. Just let the object open in both directions, past and future, and then come back to the breath, which is only now. The bell holds the time.
Knowledge of past and future. The first of the powers in book three, from samyama on how a thing changes.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE OF PAST AND FUTURE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the powers begin. Today, look at one thing the way the forester reads wood: what made it this way, and what will it become? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: The siddhis of Yoga Sutras book three are studied in yoga lineages as signs of mastery; many Hindu stories describe sages who know past and future, while many teachers caution students not to make such powers their goal.

fork.setup: you've practiced samyama for years, and you start to sense how things will turn out. what's the knowledge built on, in 3.16?
fork.reveal: 3.16: by samyama on the three transformations, knowledge of past and future. the power grows out of understanding change, yesterday's teaching.

original.note: Sanskrit atītānāgata-jñāna: knowledge (jñāna) of the past (atīta) and the not-yet-come (anāgata), 3.16.

trapdoor: what you thought: yogis claim to see the future.
what it means: the sutra says knowledge of past and future follows from samyama on how things change.
what a scholar hears: parinama-traya-samyamad atitanagata-jnanam (3.16), the first siddhi of the Vibhuti Pada, built on 3.13's three transformations.
